# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --json number,title,body,labels,comments`.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**: `gh issue create --parent <parent> ...`, or `gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child>` afterwards (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id>` (database id, as in **Blocking** below). Without sub-issues, put `Part of #<parent>` at the top of the child body.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

Infer the repo from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh api --paginate 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open' --jq '.[] | select(.author_association | IN("OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR") | not) | {number, title, author: .user.login, author_association, labels: [.labels[].name]}'`.
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Read it as in **Read an issue** above.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (see **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

- **`docs/adr/`**: read ADRs that touch the area you're about to work in. In multi-context repos, also check `src/<context>/docs/adr/` for context-scoped decisions.

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `GLOSSARY.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams: where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?" Give each proposed seam a one-line note on what it catches and what it misses.

When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

name: code-review
description: "Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes: Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/spec asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \"review since X\"."
---

Two-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:

- **Standards**: does the code conform to this repo's documented coding standards?
- **Spec**: does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / spec?

Both axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don't pollute each other's context, then this skill aggregates their findings.

The issue tracker should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Pin the fixed point

Whatever the user said is the fixed point (a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc.). If they didn't specify one, ask for it.

Capture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.

Before going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here, not inside two parallel sub-agents.

### 2. Identify the spec source

Look for the originating spec, in this order:

1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.), fetched via the workflow in the tracker doc.
2. A path the user passed as an argument.
3. A spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.
4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. If they say there isn't one, the **Spec** sub-agent will skip and report "no spec available".

### 3. Identify the standards sources

Search the repo for every file that documents how code should be written. When `CODING_STANDARDS.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md` exists, it must be on the list.

On top of whatever the repo documents, the Standards axis always carries the **smell baseline** below: a fixed set of Fowler code smells (_Refactoring_, ch.3) that applies even when a repo documents nothing. Two rules bind it:

- **The repo overrides.** A documented repo standard always wins; where it endorses something the baseline would flag, suppress the smell.
- **Always a judgement call.** Each smell is a labelled heuristic ("possible Feature Envy"), never a hard violation. Like any standard here, skip anything tooling already enforces.

Each smell reads *what it is* → *how to fix*; match it against the diff:

- **Mysterious Name**: a function, variable, or type whose name doesn't reveal what it does or holds. → rename it; if no honest name comes, the design's murky.
- **Duplicated Code**: the same logic shape appears in more than one hunk or file in the change. → extract the shared shape, call it from both.
- **Feature Envy**: a method that reaches into another object's data more than its own. → move the method onto the data it envies.
- **Data Clumps**: the same few fields or params keep travelling together (a type wanting to be born). → bundle them into one type, pass that.
- **Primitive Obsession**: a primitive or string standing in for a domain concept that deserves its own type. → give the concept its own small type.
- **Repeated Switches**: the same `switch`/`if`-cascade on the same type recurs across the change. → replace with polymorphism, or one map both sites share.
- **Shotgun Surgery**: one logical change forces scattered edits across many files in the diff. → gather what changes together into one module.
- **Divergent Change**: one file or module is edited for several unrelated reasons. → split so each module changes for one reason.
- **Speculative Generality**: abstraction, parameters, or hooks added for needs the spec doesn't have. → delete it; inline back until a real need shows.
- **Message Chains**: long `a.b().c().d()` navigation the caller shouldn't depend on. → hide the walk behind one method on the first object.
- **Middle Man**: a class or function that mostly just delegates onward. → cut it, call the real target direct.
- **Refused Bequest**: a subclass or implementer that ignores or overrides most of what it inherits. → drop the inheritance, use composition.

### 4. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel

Issue both sub-agent calls together, in the foreground, and aggregate the reports they return.

**Standards sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The full diff command and commit list.
- The list of standards-source files you found in step 3, **plus the smell baseline from step 3** pasted in full (the sub-agent has no other access to it).
- The brief: "Report, per file/hunk where relevant, (a) every place the diff violates a documented standard: cite the standard (file + the rule); and (b) any baseline smell you spot: name it and quote the hunk. Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls: documented-standard breaches can be hard, but baseline smells are always judgement calls, and a documented repo standard overrides the baseline. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words."

**Spec sub-agent prompt** should include:

- The diff command and commit list.
- The path or fetched contents of the spec.
- The brief: "Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words."

If the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.

### 5. Aggregate

Present the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings, because the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).

End with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don't pick a single winner across axes: that's the reranking the separation exists to prevent.

## Why two axes

A change can pass one axis and fail the other:

- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**
- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project's conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**

Reporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.

Implement only the core phase described here. Read the master specification first. ## 2. Inputs and first inspection

Before implementing, inspect the actual development project for existing code, `AGENTS.md`, `GLOSSARY.md`, and relevant decision records. ## 3. Settled decisions and implementation discretion

Settled requirements inherited from the master:

- Python; standard-library-only submitted engine initially.
- New independent Omok++ simulator rather than a dependency on Part 1.
- A simple reference rules path for checking the working simulator.
- Reversible transitions or equivalent restored-state behavior for future search.
- Public board values, coordinate order, rules, and total-clock semantics are fixed.
- A minimal runner and playable baseline are built early.
- Agent code is separate from offline execution, opponent code, and experiment output.
- Routine coding decisions may be made autonomously within this scope.

This phase does not retroactively select an internal board layout, class hierarchy, filenames, constructor, hash scheme, or numerical evaluator weights. The implementing AI may choose a small coherent design and document it as an implementation decision. Prefer clarity and verifiability over speculative speed optimizations. ## 4. Acceptance boundaries

These are the test seams already established in the master specification, narrowed to this phase:

| Boundary | What this phase establishes |
| --- | --- |
| Simulator rules and reversible transitions | Legal placement, captures, correct terminal results, caller-state ownership, exact restoration, and agreement with an independent reference |
| Public move-selection boundary | Explicit color, legal move return on live positions, no input mutation, a bounded baseline, and supplied-player compatibility when source files are available |
| Complete minimal game runner | Alternation, separate cumulative clocks, controlled failure reporting, recorded moves/captures, and replayable board outcomes |

Test observable results at these boundaries. Avoid tests that merely duplicate private helper expressions. Internal helper tests may support diagnosis, but they are not substitutes for these acceptance checks.

## 5. Simulator contract

### 5.1 Position ownership and validity

A position contains a 19 × 19 board and explicit side to move. External encoding is `-1` empty, `0` black, `1` white; coordinates are `(row, column)`, zero-based. The simulator must not silently interpret the board as `(x, y)`.

Support empty-board creation with black to move and loading a board with an explicitly supplied side for tactical fixtures. A fixture need not be reachable by a historical game; that does not change its geometric rule outcome. Keep structural validation distinct from optional historical reachability checks. Stone-count parity is not a reliable validation rule in this game.

When a board comes from a caller, establish owned internal state without sharing mutable rows/cells. Validate shape and cell values at external boundaries. Do not repeatedly pay for full external validation at every internal node if owned state already satisfies invariants.

Malformed input and illegal moves must fail explicitly; no wrapping negative indices, clamping coordinates, random substitution, or occupied-cell overwrite. Rejected operations leave the position unchanged. The implementing AI must document accepted integer types at the provided-player boundary based on actual source compatibility, rather than accidentally rejecting valid returned coordinates.

Terminal positions must be recognized before requesting another turn. A full terminal board has no legal move; do not fabricate a coordinate or call a player to obtain one.

### 5.2 Applying a move

For a legal move on a live position:

1. Place the moving player's stone in the selected empty cell.
2. Identify all eligible captured pairs created by that stone.
3. Remove the captured stones.
4. Evaluate exactly-five conditions for both colors on the resulting board.
5. Resolve the terminal outcome, including simultaneous wins and a full board.
6. Advance the side to move for a continuing position; expose a consistent documented transition convention for terminal positions as well.

The transition result must expose enough information to inspect the placed stone, captured cells with prior values, and resulting outcome. It must also support restoring the parent state exactly, either through a documented undo token or owned child-copy semantics. Exact return types and API names are implementation choices to record.

No rule depends on the cumulative number of captured stones. Capture statistics may be logged but must not affect victory.

### 5.3 Captures

Check all eight directed rays from the newly placed stone. A capture requires the next three cells on a ray to be:

`opponent, opponent, own`

All must be in bounds. Identify all pairs on the board after placement and before removal; then remove their union. Multiple captures are allowed. No capture occurs for a gap, three opponent stones, an absent own endpoint, or a newly placed stone in the middle of a sandwich.

There is no recursive chain capture triggered by removed cells. Do not add Pente-style capture-count victory or any variant-specific rules not present in the assignment.

### 5.4 Terminal detection

Identify maximal contiguous runs in horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal orientations. A run counts only when its length is exactly five. An overline is not a win in that direction, but it does not invalidate a separate exact-five run elsewhere or in another direction.

After captures, examine both colors. In this phase, a full-board scan is acceptable and is preferable to a clever incomplete local detector. Resolve outcomes as:

| Exact-five colors after capture resolution | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Black only | Black wins |
| White only | White wins |
| Both | Draw caused by simultaneous wins |
| Neither; no empty cells | Full-board draw |
| Neither; at least one empty cell | Continue |

Keep outcome and termination reason explicit. A capture can expose an opponent win far from the placed stone's winning line. Do not check only the mover or only lines containing the new stone.

The rules have no repetition draw or 361-move cap. Captures reopen cells. Development resource limits belong to the runner and must be labeled as experiment caps.

Implement a deliberately simple correctness reference using board copies and direct geometric checks. Its placement/capture and terminal logic must not simply delegate to the working simulator's corresponding methods; otherwise differential comparison shares the bug it is meant to detect. Sharing constants such as board dimensions is acceptable.

Reference and working engine must agree on resulting cell values, captured-cell sets, outcome, and continuing side to move. Return ordering of captured cells need not be semantically significant; compare sets and preserved values where appropriate.

Any optimized incremental state or terminal detector added now must be checked against this reference. Do not infer correctness merely because two independently named wrappers call the same helper.

### 5.6 Reversibility

Applying and undoing a legal move must restore board cells, side to move, outcome, and every maintained counter/cache/hash. Undo multiple explored children and nested transitions in reverse order. Exceptions in baseline evaluation or an early evaluation stop must not leak mutated state into the next candidate.

For copy-based transitions, demonstrate that modifying a child does not affect the parent, another child, or the external input board. Object identity does not need to match after restoration; observable state does.

### 6.1 Placement and capture geometry

- Empty board: a valid black move creates one stone, no captures, white to move, continuing outcome.
- Coordinate order: placement at `(1, 0)` changes the second row's leftmost cell only.
- Reject out-of-bounds, occupied, and malformed moves without any state change.
- Parameterize a capture from `(9, 9)` in each of the eight directions `d`: put white at `origin + d` and `origin + 2d`, black at `origin + 3d`, then place black at the origin. Remove exactly those two white cells.
- Repeat representative capture fixtures with colors swapped.
- Place eligible pairs in more than one direction from the same origin. One move must remove all eligible pairs, not just the first found.
- Exercise a capture whose endpoint lies on a board edge and a near-edge ray that exits the board. There must be no negative-index wrapping or false endpoint beyond the board.
- Replace one opponent in the pattern with an empty cell: no capture on that ray.
- Use three consecutive opponent cells before the own endpoint: no two-stone capture on that ray.
- New stone in the middle: black at `(9, 5)` and `(9, 9)`, white at `(9, 6)` and `(9, 8)`, then black at `(9, 7)`. The two whites remain.
- Capture a pair, then play a later legal stone on a removed cell. The vacancy must be reusable.

### 6.2 Exact five and overlines

- Exactly five in each orientation wins, including a run touching an edge.
- Six and longer contiguous runs are not wins by themselves. Test both extending five into six in an isolated static detector fixture and joining separated groups into six from a live position; do not ask a game runner to continue after an already-terminal five.
- Five stones with a gap do not win.
- A separate exact five still wins when the same color has an overline elsewhere.
- Both colors having exact five in a loaded static fixture is a simultaneous-win draw.

### 6.3 Capture-induced opponent victory

Initial stones:

- White at `(9, 5)` through `(9, 10)` inclusive: an overline of six.
- White at `(10, 10)`.
- Black at `(11, 10)`.

Black plays `(8, 10)`. It captures white `(9, 10)` and `(10, 10)`. White's remaining run `(9, 5)` through `(9, 9)` is exactly five. The result must be **white wins**, even though black made the move.

### 6.4 Capture-induced simultaneous wins

Use the preceding fixture and additionally place black at `(8, 6)`, `(8, 7)`, `(8, 8)`, and `(8, 9)`. Black plays `(8, 10)`.

After the same capture, black has exactly five across row 8 and white has exactly five across row 9. The result must be a **simultaneous-win draw**, not a mover win or opponent win.

### 6.5 Dense-board outcomes

Provide a documented full-board fixture with no exact-five runs and verify it independently. It must be a full-board draw. Also provide a live nearly full position where the final empty cell is filled:

- Without captures or exact five: full-board draw.
- With a capture reopening cells and no exact five: continue, rather than declaring a draw before capture resolution.

Dense fixtures are easy to get wrong. Include their generation/verification method and inspect expected capture results. Do not hardcode “draw” solely because the board was intended to be dense.

At sampled positions, explore multiple legal children and nested children, then restore the parent. Compare complete state before and after. Test consecutive captures and restoration of captured values. Log the seed and move sequence for any mismatch so it becomes a permanent minimal regression fixture.

Exact sequence counts and lengths may be selected by the implementing AI based on runtime and recorded in the verification report. The required fixture categories are not optional; a chosen large random test count does not compensate for a missing deterministic category.

Timeouts and external failures are recorded execution events, not board-rule outcomes inferred by replay.

`new own stone — opponent — opponent — existing own stone`

- A maximal contiguous run of exactly five stones wins in any of the four line orientations.
- A run of six or more is not a win merely because it contains a five-cell substring.
- Captures can shorten the opponent's overline into exactly five, making the opponent the winner after the mover's action.
- If both colors have exactly five after the move, the result is a draw.
- If neither color wins and the board is full after captures, the result is a draw.

The agent must work without importing the offline harness or depending on the user's Part 1 game manager. Caller-owned board objects must remain unchanged. 2. Candidate move generation.
3. Strong move ordering.

6. Game-wide time management controlling the search budget.

- Offensive opportunity and defensive urgency.

Decide concrete allocation formulas only after measuring speed and game-length behavior. Low-time operation must still return legal moves reliably.

Keep their files and dependencies separate from submission code and control their execution through the harness.

Assign opponents to training, validation, and final holdout pools. Exact sizes depend on what is available; no fixed percentages are selected.

- Training opponents drive candidate fitness and mutation selection.
- Validation opponents provide periodic checks of generalization and regressions.
- Final holdout opponents remain unused for tuning and version selection until the final evaluation.

Measure each color separately and inspect weak matchups, not just aggregate league scores. Classmate results and synthetic-opponent results are evidence about local strength, not proof of actual class rank.

Offline optimization mutates/selects evaluation parameters and selected search parameters. Candidates play a diverse league rather than only the current champion. Retain historical champions to detect forgetting and nontransitive matchups.

Potential tunables are pattern/capture weights, offense/defense balance, candidate generation parameters, ordering coefficients, tactical extension thresholds, and time allocation parameters. Exact parameter schema, bounds, mutation operators, league weights, and promotion thresholds belong to the evolution phase.

"""Owned, immutable positions and copy-based Omok++ transitions."""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Board = tuple[tuple[int, ...], ...]
Outcome = Literal['ongoing', 'black_win', 'white_win', 'draw']
Reason = Literal['exact_five', 'simultaneous_wins', 'full_board']


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class CapturedCell:
    cell: Coordinate
    prior_value: int


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Position:
    board: Board
    side_to_move: int
    outcome: Outcome = 'ongoing'
    reason: Reason | None = None

    @classmethod
    def empty(cls) -> 'Position':
        return cls(tuple((EMPTY,) * SIZE for _ in range(SIZE)), BLACK)

    def play(self, move: Coordinate) -> 'Transition':
        row, col = move
        board = [list(values) for values in self.board]
        board[row][col] = self.side_to_move
        child = Position(tuple(tuple(values) for values in board), 1 - self.side_to_move)
        return Transition(child, move, self.side_to_move, ())


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Transition:
    position: Position
    move: Coordinate
    color: int
    captured: tuple[CapturedCell, ...]

# AI-written by OpenAI Codex (GPT-6), for issue #3.
"""Seeded legal sequences, child isolation checks, and replayable mismatches."""
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
import random
import time
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any

from omok.simulator import Coordinate, Position, SIZE, EMPTY
from verification.reference import ReferencePosition


def legal_moves(board: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> list[Coordinate]:
    return [(r, c) for r in range(SIZE) for c in range(SIZE) if board[r][c] == EMPTY]


def state(position: Position | ReferencePosition) -> tuple[object, ...]:
    return (tuple(tuple(row) for row in position.board), position.side_to_move,
            position.outcome, position.reason)


def choose_move(position: Position, rng: random.Random, biased: bool) -> Coordinate:
    moves = legal_moves(position.board)
    if not biased:
        return rng.choice(moves)
    capture_moves = []
    for r, c in moves:
        for dr in (-1, 0, 1):
            for dc in (-1, 0, 1):
                if not (dr or dc):
                    continue
                end_r, end_c = r + 3 * dr, c + 3 * dc
                if (0 <= end_r < SIZE and 0 <= end_c < SIZE
                        and position.board[r + dr][c + dc] == 1 - position.side_to_move
                        and position.board[r + 2 * dr][c + 2 * dc] == 1 - position.side_to_move
                        and position.board[end_r][end_c] == position.side_to_move):
                    capture_moves.append((r, c))
                    break
            else:
                continue
            break
    if capture_moves:
        return rng.choice(capture_moves)
    # Concentrate fallback play around existing stones to create capture opportunities.
    nearby = [(r, c) for r, c in moves if any(
        0 <= r + dr < SIZE and 0 <= c + dc < SIZE
        and position.board[r + dr][c + dc] != EMPTY
        for dr in (-1, 0, 1) for dc in (-1, 0, 1))]
    return rng.choice(nearby or moves)


def checked_move(position: Position, reference: ReferencePosition, move: Coordinate,
                 seed: int, mode: str, history: list[Coordinate],
                 failure_dir: Path) -> tuple[Position, ReferencePosition, int]:
    before, ref_before = state(position), state(reference)
    try:
        actual = position.play(move)
        expected = reference.play(move)
        if state(actual.position) != state(expected.position):
            raise AssertionError('Board, side, outcome, or reason mismatch.')
        if {item.cell: item.prior_value for item in actual.captured} != {
                item.cell: item.prior_value for item in expected.captured}:
            raise AssertionError('Captured cells/prior values mismatch.')
        if state(position) != before or state(reference) != ref_before:
            raise AssertionError('Parent state mutated.')
    except Exception as error:
        failure_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        path = failure_dir / f'mismatch-{mode}-{seed}.json'
        path.write_text(json.dumps({
            'seed': seed, 'mode': mode, 'moves': history + [move],
            'initial_board': Position.empty().board, 'initial_side': 0,
            'before': before, 'reference_before': ref_before,
            'error': repr(error),
        }, indent=2) + '\n')
        raise AssertionError(f'Differential failure; replay moves in {path}') from error
    return actual.position, expected.position, len(actual.captured)


def run_sequences(sequences: int = 16, max_moves: int = 240, seed: int = 20261008,
                  failure_dir: Path = Path('.scratch/differential')) -> dict[str, Any]:
    records = []
    checked = 0
    started = time.perf_counter()
    for mode in ('ordinary', 'capture_biased'):
        for number in range(sequences):
            sequence_seed = seed + number + (100000 if mode == 'capture_biased' else 0)
            rng = random.Random(sequence_seed)
            position = Position.empty()
            reference = ReferencePosition.empty()
            history: list[Coordinate] = []
            captured_count = 0
            for ply in range(max_moves):
                if position.outcome != 'ongoing':
                    break
                if ply % 20 == 0:
                    snapshot = state(position)
                    siblings = []
                    for move in rng.sample(legal_moves(position.board),
                                           min(3, len(legal_moves(position.board)))):
                        child, ref_child, _ = checked_move(
                            position, reference, move, sequence_seed, mode, history, failure_dir)
                        checked += 1
                        siblings.append((child, state(child)))
                        if child.outcome == 'ongoing':
                            nested_move = rng.choice(legal_moves(child.board))
                            checked_move(child, ref_child, nested_move, sequence_seed, mode,
                                         history + [move], failure_dir)
                            checked += 1
                    if state(position) != snapshot or any(state(child) != saved for child, saved in siblings):
                        raise AssertionError('Parent/sibling isolation failure.')
                move = choose_move(position, rng, mode == 'capture_biased')
                position, reference, captured = checked_move(
                    position, reference, move, sequence_seed, mode, history, failure_dir)
                checked += 1
                captured_count += captured
                history.append(move)
            records.append({'mode': mode, 'seed': sequence_seed, 'moves': len(history),
                            'captured_stones': captured_count, 'outcome': position.outcome,
                            'reason': position.reason,
                            'stopped': 'terminal' if position.outcome != 'ongoing' else 'verification_cap'})
    return {'sequences_per_mode': sequences, 'max_moves': max_moves,
            'checked_transitions': checked, 'elapsed_seconds': time.perf_counter() - started,
            'records': records}


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--sequences', type=int, default=16)
    parser.add_argument('--max-moves', type=int, default=240)
    parser.add_argument('--seed', type=int, default=20261008)
    parser.add_argument('--failure-dir', type=Path, default=Path('.scratch/differential'))
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.sequences < 1 or args.max_moves < 1:
        parser.error('Sequence and move counts must be positive.')
    print(json.dumps(run_sequences(args.sequences, args.max_moves, args.seed, args.failure_dir), indent=2))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

# Simulator contract and implementation decision

Chosen for issue #3 on 2026-10-08: immutable owned board copies, with full-board
terminal detection. This is a new engine; the professor's players are unchanged.

```python
from omok.simulator import Position

parent = Position.empty()                  # black to move
transition = parent.play((1, 0))           # row, column, zero-based
child = transition.position
assert parent.board[1][0] == -1
assert child.board[1][0] == 0

fixture = Position([[ -1 ] * 19 for _ in range(19)], side_to_move=1)
```

`Position(board, side_to_move)` copies and validates a 19 × 19 rectangular
sequence, normalizes cell values, and detects its outcome immediately. It accepts
fixture positions regardless of historical reachability or stone-count parity.
The caller must supply color; it is never inferred. Board values are -1 empty,
0 black, 1 white. The primary maintained state is exactly `board`, `side_to_move`,
`outcome`, and `reason`. The board is a tuple of tuple rows; the position and
transition records are frozen. No counters, hashes, caches, or history are maintained.

Cells, color, and coordinates accept Python integers and objects supporting the
integer `__index__` protocol; booleans, floats (even 0.0), and strings are rejected.
Both provided players return tuples of built-in integer coordinates and index
board rows directly. No concrete NumPy array requirement appears in their source.
This establishes compatibility with their visible indexing/coordinate behavior,
not with the absent official Player class or an unknown grader environment.

`play((row, column))` requires a live position and empty in-bounds target, otherwise
raises `ValueError` without state change. Its result exposes:

- `move`: normalized row/column tuple.
- `color`: the mover's explicit color.
- `captured`: sorted immutable records with `cell` and `prior_value`.
- `position`: the independent resulting position with explicit outcome and reason.

The engine copies rows, places the stone, collects all qualifying pairs from the
post-placement board in eight rays, removes their union, then checks maximal runs
for both colors in four orientations. Exactly five wins; overlines alone do not.
No recursive captures, capture-count win, repetition draw, or move limit exists.
Internal child creation skips external board validation because its cells are
already owned and valid; it still performs full terminal detection.

| Outcome | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| `ongoing` | `None` |
| `black_win`, `white_win` | `exact_five` |
| `draw` | `simultaneous_wins` or `full_board` |

A continuing child advances side to the opponent. A terminal child retains the
mover's side, including opponent victories and draws. A loaded terminal fixture
retains its explicitly supplied side. Search must check `outcome` before interpreting
side or expanding children. `play` rejects every terminal position.

To return from a child, retain the unchanged parent reference. Sibling and nested
transitions cannot modify it. To modify a board for another fixture or a player,
create `[list(row) for row in position.board]` and load a new Position if needed.
There is no mutable make/unmake or undo token. Tests inspect every maintained field,
external inputs, rejected moves, consecutive captures, multiple siblings, nested
children, and modified exported snapshots at this public seam.

## Independent reference

`verification.reference.ReferencePosition` implements the same observable
position/transition vocabulary. It enumerates all length-four windows in the four
undirected orientations, accepts the newly placed cell only at either endpoint,
and collects the matching windows before removal. Its terminal detector constructs
complete rows, columns, and diagonals and groups equal cells with `itertools.groupby`.
It never calls the engine's capture or terminal helpers. Shared constants, typing
aliases, and the captured-cell value record do not contain rule logic.

The same literal deterministic expectations run against each implementation;
differential sequences additionally compare every board cell, captured cell/prior
value, outcome, reason, and side. Captures do not count toward victory.

## Independently verified dense fixtures

Generate the full board as `board[r][c] = ((r + 2*c) % 4) // 2` for 0 ≤ r,c < 19.
Along the four orientations, the residue advances by 2, 1, 3, or -1 modulo four.
The horizontal colors alternate; the other orientations have runs of at most two.
Thus no maximal five exists, and the full board is a draw. Both the run-start
engine scan and independently grouped reference lines verify this construction.

For final-placement fixtures, remove `(0, 0)`:

- Black fills it: the only qualifying ray is down-right. `(1, 1)` and `(2, 2)`
  are white and `(3, 3)` is black. Those two cells become vacant and play continues.
  Removal cannot extend any remaining run, so it cannot create a five here.
- White fills it: no capture. Horizontal and down-right first cells are white;
  downward starts black, white, white, which is not a captured pair. Changing
  the corner extends the down-right white run to three, not five. The board is
  a full-board draw.

Tests repeat these constructions with colors complemented, explicitly asserting
starting live status, exact captured sets, outcome, and reason at both rule seams.
